summary:
Consensual same-sex intimacy between adults is not a criminal offence in Antigua and Barbuda. On 5 July 2022 the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court, in Orden David et al v The Attorney General of Antigua and Barbuda, declared Sections 12 and 15 of the Sexual Offences Act 1995 unconstitutional and void. Before that ruling, adult-on-adult buggery carried up to fifteen years' imprisonment, five years where a minor committed the act, and life where an adult committed it against a minor; 'serious indecency' carried up to ten years where the target was a child under sixteen, and repeat offenders convicted of buggery were placed on the Sex Offenders Register for life.

The same judgment read the constitutional prohibition on sex discrimination as covering sexual orientation and gender identity. That interpretive holding does not function as a statutory protection regime: Antiguan law still does not address discrimination or harassment on account of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no explicit antidiscrimination protections exist in legislation.

Trans visitors have no route to legal recognition of gender identity. There is no mechanism to change a legal gender marker; only name changes are available. A passport or identification document showing a gender inconsistent with presentation will therefore stand unremedied for the duration of a visit, and there is no sourced pathway for a visitor to resolve that mismatch.

Same-sex unions are not recognised in any form. Households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same rights afforded to opposite-sex married couples, so a partner cannot rely on marriage-based entry, inheritance, hospital-visitation or next-of-kin standing.

Violence against LGBTQ people has been documented rather than merely alleged. Orden David, the Antiguan activist who brought the constitutional challenge, was bullied and physically attacked before the ruling, including being struck on the head and knocked out in daylight. Advocacy litigation in the region has argued that buggery and indecency laws stigmatise and legitimise hate speech, discrimination and violence, and that framing remains the backdrop against which street-level hostility occurs despite decriminalisation.

Official hostility is part of the recorded record. At the May 2016 Universal Periodic Review, several governments urged Antigua and Barbuda to repeal the sodomy ban and guarantee full human rights to LGBTQ people; the government announced on 24 August 2016 that it had no intention of repealing the ban, while acknowledging that a lawsuit would most likely strike it down on the basis of the identical jurisprudence from Belize. Human Rights Watch reported the 2022 decriminalisation ruling, and Outright International's country overview, updated March 2026, still records the absence of antidiscrimination protection and of legal gender recognition.
tangentialFactors:
Antigua and Barbuda sits within a region in transition. As of the 2023 reporting, six Caribbean countries still criminalise same-sex conduct, and a visitor crossing from a neighbouring jurisdiction may enter a materially different legal regime without any change in practical surroundings.

The litigation that produced the 2022 ruling was announced on 1 November 2019 by the Eastern Caribbean Alliance for Diversity and Equality, which had stated in December 2019 that it would file court challenges to buggery and indecency laws in Barbados, St Kitts-Nevis, Antigua and Barbuda, Grenada and Saint Lucia. The regional character of that campaign means the Antiguan outcome is one data point in a wider judicial pattern rather than an isolated exception.

The Advocates for Human Rights lodged a submission to the UN Human Rights Committee in January 2025 listing the LGBTQ+ rights issues Antigua and Barbuda still faces ahead of its review, which indicates that decriminalisation left substantive questions open before international scrutiny.

Statements made to the UN Human Rights Council in 2016 were divided: the Minister of Social Transformation, Samantha Marshall, called the ban antiquated and said it should be repealed, while Parliamentary Secretary Maureen Payne-Hyman assured the Council that LGBTQ people are not persecuted in the country. Visitors should not read either statement as a settled guarantee of treatment on the ground.
localsOnly:
Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination or harassment based on sexual orientation or gender identity, notwithstanding the constitutional reading adopted in 2022. Complaints of workplace, housing or service denial on those grounds have no dedicated statute to invoke.

Same-sex couples cannot marry or register a union in any form, and their households do not receive the rights granted to opposite-sex married couples.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable. Only name changes can be effected; there is no procedure for amending the gender marker on identity documents, which affects employment, banking, healthcare and interactions with the police and immigration authorities.

Domestic advocacy has driven the legal changes on record. Orden David's constitutional challenge succeeded in 2022, and the Eastern Caribbean Alliance for Diversity and Equality announced the regional challenge programme that led to it. National groups continue to raise the outstanding SOGI-protection questions before UN treaty bodies.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved in the sources: whether the 2022 ruling is consistently applied by police and prosecutors in practice, and whether any charges under Sections 12 or 15 have been brought or dropped since July 2022. No enforcement data is available here.

Not sourced: whether any legislation on hate-crime enhancement, conversion-therapy prohibition or relationship recognition has been introduced or enacted after the March 2026 update of the Outright International overview.

Not sourced: any trans-specific provision on access to gender-affirming healthcare, on customs or border treatment of hormone medication, or on the evidentiary standard applied when a traveller's documents do not match their presentation.

Unresolved: the scope of the constitutional sex-discrimination reading in litigation. The sources record the interpretive holding but do not document a decided case applying it to a discrimination complaint.

Not sourced: any recent travel advisories or reported incidents involving trans visitors specifically, as distinct from LGBTQ residents.
